messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan is a 75-year-old South Asian man who came to the United States as a refugee decades ago, carrying with him a history that had never fully resolved into the past. He is married, soft-spoken, and has spent the better part of his adult life in America as a potter — a craft he brought from his homeland, one that once gave his days both structure and meaning. He presented for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 50, describing a constellation of symptoms that had worsened quietly over recent years until they could no longer be managed in silence.

The events that fractured Rajan's sense of safety occurred during the violence and forced displacement of his early life. He witnessed the deaths of people he loved — bodies carried past him, makeshift burials in disturbed earth, the sounds of vehicles and shouting that preceded raids on his village. Police and soldiers moved through his community with authority that meant terror rather than protection. The chaos was not a single event but an accumulated season of loss, and much of what Rajan experienced during that time has never organized itself into a coherent narrative. He reports that his memories of the period come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together — sensory fragments, images without context, a feeling of cold ground beneath his feet that arrives without any story attached. What he experienced was so overwhelming that he cannot seem to put it into words even now, though the memories themselves feel more real and vivid than anything from his ordinary life since.

It is precisely this quality of his memory — raw, wordless, and fragmented — that keeps the past so close to the surface. When a memory intrudes, it does not arrive as a recollection but as a reliving, and in its wake Rajan finds himself scanning his surroundings compulsively, reading every doorway and parking lot for signs of threat. This hypervigilant checking, which has become a near-constant feature of his daily life, reinforces his deepest fear: that he is no longer capable of being safe, that the world remains fundamentally dangerous, and that he lacks the inner resources to cope with even minor disturbances. His belief that he must be especially careful because you never know what can happen next is not an abstract worry but a felt certainty, one the fragmentary memories keep renewing.

These negative appraisals, in turn, make the memories harder to bear and easier to trigger. When Rajan believes he is incapable and perpetually at risk, any sensory echo of the original violence lands with amplified force. A car engine revving in the street outside his pottery studio is enough — the sound pulls him back before he can orient himself, his hands going still over the clay. Police cars, even parked ones he passes on his walk from the parking lot, send a current of alarm through him that takes hours to subside. Funerals are perhaps the most destabilizing: a neighbor's bereavement gathering last spring, with its gathering of dark-clothed figures and its proximity to a cemetery, left him unable to work for several days. The triggers, fed by the appraisals that have settled into his thinking like sediment, arrive with a frequency that exhausts him.

Over the years, Rajan has organized his life around avoidance in ways that have quietly narrowed it. He steers away from any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, which has meant withdrawing from community organizations he once valued. More painfully, he has begun avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful — celebrations, his grandchildren's recitals — because he has come to believe that positive feeling is a kind of exposure, a lowering of the guard that something terrible will punish. These avoidances have not brought relief; instead, they have deepened his conviction that he is fragile and diminished, that the man who once shaped vessels with steady hands is gone. The avoidance itself becomes a trigger for new intrusions, each retreat confirming that the world outside is as dangerous as he fears.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him gently that she was losing him — not to death, but to disappearance. He arrived at intake hoping, tentatively, that some part of what he had been might still be recoverable. What he fears most is that it cannot be.
